Where did this strange hookah come from here?
Hookah has long become part of French culture.
We are a French restaurant, not a noisy bar!
Vitya, do not shout, our restaurant is changing.
Why change what is already working excellently?
Life requires moving forward and fresh ideas.
I will not allow ruining my dear kitchen!
You promised me complete freedom in the hall yourself.
That is it, I am calling Nagiyev right now!
Call, the owner will fully support this new plan.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bar, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Проверьте все бары и старых друзей.
examples.trans: Check all the bars and old friends.
It is already morning. Our bar is closing.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Prefix 'вз-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'яться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to appear', forming an aspectual pair with 'браться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: Where did the goose come from?
Where did this goose come from?
Where did it come from in the cream?

meanings.note: direction: идти вперёд = to go forward
colloquial, like a preposition + genitive: лезть вперёд кого-то = to push in ahead of someone
Secondary conversational sense ('forward!, let's go!') (as a command) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Вы взяточник! Вы лезете вперёд больного ребёнка.
examples.trans: You're a bribe-taker! You're pushing in ahead of a sick child.

examples.text: Ну же, смелее вперёд, шеф ждёт твоего ответа!
examples.trans: Come on, boldly forward, the chef is waiting for your answer!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'stupidly'.
Secondary conversational sense ('it's stupid') (as a predicate: Это глупо.) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
+ infinitive: давай убирать = let's clean up
Secondary conversational sense ('come on') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('bye, see you') (casual goodbye) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

related.gloss: to give (the verb it comes from)

давно.gloss: for a long time; long ago

meanings.note: with present: Я давно здесь = I've been here a long time
Secondary conversational sense ('long ago') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You haven't been interested in me for a long time.

examples.text: Вспомнил? Я давно тебя не интересую.
examples.trans: Now you remember? You haven't been interested in me for a long time.

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'movement, traffic' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('traffic') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: A smooth motion of the hand.

examples.text: Стой спокойно и не делай резких движений.
examples.trans: Stand calmly and do not make sharp movements.

meanings.note: to a loved one, and at the start of letters
to a loved one, and at the start of letters

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

meanings.note: in threats: ты ещё увидишь = you'll see
Secondary conversational sense ('still, yet') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('even (with comparatives)') (ещё больше = even more) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.
Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('living room') (regional/colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'what for'.

examples.trans: Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

звонить.gloss: to call, to phone; to ring

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'позвонить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to ring') (a bell or phone) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'idea' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Хорошая идея! Я сейчас же попробую.
examples.trans: Good idea! I will try right now.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hookah', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: They smoke hookah in the restaurant.

examples.text: Откуда здесь взялся этот странный кальян?
examples.trans: Where did this strange hookah come from here?

examples.text: Кальян давно стал частью французской культуры.
examples.trans: Hookah has long become part of French culture.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to shout', forming an aspectual pair with 'крикнуть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Не надо кричать. Хорошо, я буду сегодня.
examples.trans: There's no need to shout. All right, I'll be there tonight.

meanings.note: arts, literature, and social refinement

examples.text: Здравствуйте всем! Я ваш новый редактор культуры.
examples.trans: Hello everyone! I am your new culture editor.

examples.text: Но людям также нужна высокая культура!
examples.trans: But people also need high culture!

examples.text: Высокая культура не приносит высокие рейтинги.
examples.trans: High culture does not bring high ratings.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: 'менять что на что' = to swap something for something
Secondary conversational sense ('to change') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll swap an iPhone for a phone.

examples.text: Славик, смотри сюда. Меняю свой новый айфон на твой старый телефон.
examples.trans: Slavik, look here. I'll swap my new iPhone for your old phone.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to change', forming an aspectual pair with 'поменяться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: Да, люди вокруг меняются к лучшему.
examples.trans: Yes, people around are changing for the better.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: + dative of the person: обещать вам

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'куда').

examples.trans: Where does that word come from?
Thief, thief. Where does that word come from?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.
Secondary conversational sense ('great!, excellent!') (as a one-word reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I know this town really well!

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'личный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('excellent').

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: перестань(те)! = stop it!, oh come on!

examples.text: Да перестаньте! Я двадцать лет в карты не играла.
examples.trans: Oh, stop it! I haven't played cards for twenty years.

examples.text: Иначе я перестану давать тебе деньги!
examples.trans: Otherwise I'll stop giving you money!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'plan' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The mayor came up with a new plan.

examples.text: Но мэр придумал новый план. Сосед мэра теперь пойдёт в мэры.
examples.trans: But the mayor came up with a new plan. The mayor's neighbour will now run for mayor.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'держать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to support, to back', paired with 'поддерживать'.

examples.trans: If you support me, we will break through.
The friends decided to support Samson.

examples.text: Короче, мужики! Если поддержите меня, мы прорвёмся.
examples.trans: In short, guys! If you support me, we will break through.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'зволить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to allow', forming an aspectual pair with 'позволять'.

examples.trans: Allow me, I'll make it more comfortable.

examples.text: Прошу, присаживайтесь. Позвольте, я сделаю удобнее.
examples.trans: Please, have a seat. Allow me, I'll make it more comfortable.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'completely'.

examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna has paid off the debt in full.

examples.text: Насколько нам известно, Марина Сергеевна полностью закрыла долг.
examples.trans: As far as we know, Marina Sergeyevna has paid off the debt in full.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'full' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('complete, total, utter') (полный кошмар = a total nightmare) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: На столе стоял полный стакан воды.
examples.trans: A full glass of water stood on the table.

examples.text: Ну что я тебе скажу, Аркаша? Это полный кошмар!
examples.trans: Well, what can I tell you, Arkasha? This is a total nightmare!

meanings.note: портить настроение = ruin someone's mood

examples.text: Так, не портите мне прекрасное настроение.
examples.trans: Right, don't ruin my wonderful mood.

examples.text: Поверьте, вам это не надо. Вы так карму портите.
examples.trans: Believe us, you do not need this. You ruin your karma that way.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'straight'.
Secondary conversational sense ('straight ahead') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: В смысле, Виктор Степанович? Прямо так, да?
examples.trans: What do you mean, Viktor Stepanovich? Just like that?

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'fresh', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Свежие ягоды, кофе! У вас тут романтический завтрак.
examples.trans: Fresh berries, coffee! You are having a romantic breakfast here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вобода'). Common feminine noun meaning 'freedom, liberty' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Right now there's freedom, cars, the sea!
He was released (came out to freedom).

examples.text: Ну выйдешь ты через десять лет, и что? А сейчас свобода, машины, море!
examples.trans: Well, you'll get out in ten years, and then what? Right now there's freedom, cars, the sea!

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: + instrumental: стал сентиментальным
Secondary conversational sense ('to start (doing)') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты слишком сентиментальным стал. А лидер должен быть жёстким.
examples.trans: You've become too sentimental. And a leader has to be tough.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'wall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: The picture is on the wall.

examples.text: Не надо врать. Стену монастыря сносят!
examples.trans: Don't lie. They're pulling down the monastery wall!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange, odd').
'а то' at the start of a sentence: 'а то мы уже начали беспокоиться' = we were starting to worry

examples.text: А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: We were starting to worry, you see.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

meanings.note: + genitive or accusative: требую тишины

examples.trans: We demand that house arrest be replaced.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'toilet', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: The toilet is in the corridor.
Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

убрать.gloss: to remove, to take away; to tidy up

meanings.en: to remove, to take away, to cut out
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'брать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to remove', forming an aspectual pair with 'убирать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to clean up, to tidy') (a room) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты можешь убрать весь этот шум?
examples.trans: Can you cut out all this noise?
Take the phone off the table.

examples.text: Так, ты можешь убрать весь этот шум? Нам нужен только Аникеев.
examples.trans: Right, can you cut out all this noise? We only need Anikeev.

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('French').

examples.trans: And you're drinking French cognac yourself.

meanings.note: person who owns a business or property
Secondary conversational sense ('host') (person receiving guests) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The owner of the restaurant came out into the dining room.
The restaurant owner personally greets the guests.
The owner is busy in the kitchen for now.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'part', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('military or police unit') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I kept my part of the deal.
This is the best part of the book.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, я выполнил свою часть сделки.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I kept my part of the deal.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('noisy, loud').

examples.trans: We turned off all noisy equipment.

examples.text: Шеф, мы уже выключили все шумные приборы.
examples.trans: Chef, we have already turned off all noisy equipment.

examples.text: Мы французский ресторан, а не шумный бар!
examples.trans: We are a French restaurant, not a noisy bar!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to joke', paired with 'пошутить'.

examples.text: Шутишь? Правда, скажи, где деньги? Меня наняли.
examples.trans: Are you joking? Seriously, tell me, where's the money? They hired me.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
